name: Windsor Blue
lede: Windsor blue is a muted purplish blue; the name is best known as an artists' paint trade name, but the swatch here comes from an older color chart.

sections.title: Two things called Windsor blue
sections.body:
Paterson's dictionary lists "Windsor blue" and "Winsor blue" as other names for Monastral blue, a very durable synthetic blue pigment first identified by ICI in 1928 by accident, now better known as phthalocyanine blue [1]. Winsor is also the name of the paint maker Winsor & Newton, and the dictionary says the spelling is a trade name of that company [1].

Our swatch is a different thing. It is a moderate purplish blue from the Maerz and Paul dictionary of 1930, plate 44, with a first record of 1912 [2]. It is much duller and greyer than a phthalocyanine blue, so do not assume the two match [2].

sections.title: In paintings
sections.body: A color near this swatch appears in 100 of 23,781 paintings, as photographed, and it peaks in the 1900s at 3.3 times the museums' baseline [3]. Matisse is the most devoted painter, in 4 of 50 works [3]. It is a plain purplish blue, a near neighbor of [[indigo]] in hue and much lighter [2].

origin.named_after: a spelling of Winsor, the trade name of Winsor & Newton, for phthalocyanine blue; undocumented for the chart color
origin.source: Paterson, A Dictionary of Colour; ColorHub library

disambiguation.gloss: a dye blue, not the synthetic pigment blue called Windsor

notes.cite: Paterson, A Dictionary of Colour, p. 267 ("Monastral blue")

questions.q: Which pigment does Paterson say Windsor blue is another name for?
In what year was Monastral blue first identified by ICI, by accident?

openers: Monastral blue was found by accident at ICI in 1928, and Windsor blue is one of its trade names.
